opus-5.5.text:
Well, this goes back to something people have noticed since the early days of AI, often called Moravec's paradox. The things that feel hard to us, like playing chess at a grandmaster level, doing calculus, or proving theorems, turned out to be relatively easy to get machines to do. And the things that feel effortless, like recognizing a friend's face across a crowded room, walking over uneven ground, understanding a joke, or knowing that if you push a glass off a table it will probably break, turned out to be enormously difficult.

I think the reason is that our sense of what's hard is really a sense of what requires conscious effort. When I do long division, I'm aware of every step, so it feels like work. But when I look at a scene and understand it, all of that processing is happening below awareness. It was refined over hundreds of millions of years of evolution and then over years of embodied experience as a child. So it feels easy precisely because it's so deeply built in, not because it's computationally simple.

This matters a lot right now, because we're constantly tempted to read a system's performance on some impressive-seeming task as evidence of general intelligence. A language model passes the bar exam or a medical licensing test, and people conclude it must have the understanding a human lawyer or doctor has. But those tests were designed for humans, and they implicitly assume all the common sense, the grounded understanding of the world, that any human test-taker brings along. They don't test that, because for people it doesn't need testing. A machine can do well on the part we think is hard while lacking the foundation we take for granted, and that shows up as brittleness, strange errors, and failure to generalize when the situation shifts even a little.

So I'd argue we need to be much more careful in how we evaluate these systems. Rather than asking "Can it do this thing that's hard for humans?", we should ask "What mechanisms is it using, and do they reflect the kind of robust, abstract, generalizable understanding we actually care about?" Our intuitions about difficulty were tuned to other humans, and applying them to a very different kind of mind leads us astray.

fable-5.1.text:
Because our intuitions about difficulty are calibrated on humans, not on machines, and the two can have almost inverted difficulty profiles. When we look at a task and say "that's hard," what we usually mean is that it's hard for a person — it requires a lot of conscious effort, training, deliberate reasoning. Playing chess at a grandmaster level, doing symbolic integration, proving theorems. Those feel like the pinnacle of intelligence to us. And then the things that feel trivial — recognizing that a cat is still a cat when it's partly behind a couch, understanding that if I knock over a glass the water will spill, following a simple conversation with a three-year-old — those don't feel like intelligence at all. They feel like just... being awake.

But that feeling is an artifact of our own cognitive architecture. The things that feel effortless to us feel that way precisely because evolution spent hundreds of millions of years optimizing them. Perception, motor control, basic physical and social intuition — all of that is running on enormously sophisticated machinery that's completely hidden from introspection. You don't experience the computation; you just see the cat. Whereas chess is a recent cultural invention we have no specialized hardware for, so we feel every bit of the strain. This is Moravec's paradox, and it's been around since the 1980s, but I think we keep relearning it because the intuition is so stubborn.

So when people in the field made predictions — and they made them repeatedly — that once we'd cracked chess or calculus, the "easy" stuff like common sense would follow shortly, they had it exactly backwards. The easy stuff was the hard part. And I'd argue the pattern is still with us. Today's systems can write passable poetry and pass bar exams, and people take that as evidence of general intelligence because those are things that are hard for us. Meanwhile the same systems can fail at tasks that any child handles — keeping track of what's physically possible, noticing that a question is nonsensical, generalizing a concept to a slightly different situation. If you use human difficulty as your yardstick, you'll systematically overestimate what these systems understand, because you'll be impressed by the wrong things and fail to test the things that actually matter.

astra-6.text:
Well, our intuitions about difficulty are based on what’s hard for us, and that doesn’t necessarily line up with what’s hard for a machine. We think of playing chess or doing advanced mathematics as requiring tremendous intelligence. But recognizing an everyday situation, understanding a casual remark, or figuring out how to pick up an unfamiliar object feels effortless. We don’t notice how much intelligence those activities involve because so much of it happens unconsciously.

That’s the paradox: some things we regard as intellectually demanding have turned out to be relatively amenable to computers, while things a young child can do remain very challenging. So when a system does something that impresses us, we’re tempted to assume it must also have mastered the abilities we consider more basic. But that inference doesn’t follow. Our own sense of difficulty isn’t a reliable map of the abilities a machine has—or of how those abilities fit together.

sol-6.1.text:
We tend to judge difficulty by what requires conscious effort for us. Playing chess or solving a calculus problem seems hard, while recognizing an object or understanding a simple story seems easy. But those apparently easy things draw on an enormous amount of knowledge and processing that we don’t have conscious access to.

That’s part of what’s called Moravec’s paradox: some things that are difficult for humans turn out to be relatively tractable for computers, while things that young children do effortlessly remain very challenging. So our own sense of effort is a poor guide to the computational difficulty of a task. And success on something we consider intellectually demanding doesn’t necessarily imply that a system has the more basic, flexible understanding we take for granted.
